Carnegie Mellon University: Flagship Website Redesign & Distributed CMS Implementation
Carnegie Mellon University partnered with Carnegie Higher Ed for design strategy and Knectar for technical implementation to completely reimagine their digital presence. This 18-month initiative resulted in a modern, scalable website ecosystem built on a distributed CMS architecture using GitLab and Pantheon Upstream, supporting both the flagship CMU.edu site and multiple unit sites across the university.

Key Objectives
The primary goal was to modernize Carnegie Mellon's digital brand presence while creating a scalable, distributed content management system that could serve the diverse needs of the university's many departments and units. The project aimed to streamline development workflows and governance processes that had become cumbersome over time, while significantly improving the user experience across all university digital touchpoints. Perhaps most importantly, the new system needed to enable autonomous content management for individual units while maintaining strict brand consistency across the entire university ecosystem.

Technical Architecture
Infrastructure & Deployment
• Version Control: GitLab-based development workflow
• Hosting: Pantheon Upstream architecture
• Deployment Model: Merge request/pull request workflow with internal CMU dev team code review
• Scalability: Component-based architecture supporting flagship and unit sites

Development Workflow
The development process follows a collaborative model where the Knectar team develops features and components before submitting merge requests to Carnegie Mellon's internal development team. Each submission undergoes a thorough code review process conducted by CMU's technical staff, ensuring that all changes meet the university's standards for security, performance, and maintainability. Once approved, changes are merged into the production pipeline, creating a seamless flow from development to deployment. This approach maintains ongoing collaboration between external development expertise and internal institutional knowledge, supporting both rapid innovation and careful oversight.

Design System & Component Architecture
Comprehensive Component Library
The implementation features 50+ specialized components designed to work across multiple site contexts:

Core Navigation & Structure
The foundation of the system rests on a sophisticated multi-level header system that adapts seamlessly between flagship and unit site variations. The responsive navigation incorporates both utility and primary menu systems, ensuring users can access essential information regardless of their entry point into the university's digital ecosystem. A globally managed emergency alert system provides the university with the ability to communicate critical information instantly across all sites, while sticky navigation and integrated search functionality enhance user experience by keeping essential tools accessible as users explore content.

Content Components
The content architecture centers around flexible hero variations that adapt to different contexts, from the flagship homepage hero featuring dynamic video backgrounds to specialized landing page heroes integrated with request-for-information forms and program-specific presentations. Feature panels offer sophisticated layout options with left or right media placement and light or dark variations, providing content creators with the tools to create visually compelling narratives. The stats panels bring data to life through animated statistics combined with testimonials and faculty spotlights, while various router systems including visual grids, lists, and panels create intuitive navigation pathways. The interactive timeline slider serves as a particularly innovative component, allowing the university to showcase its rich history and ongoing evolution in an engaging, visual format.

Specialized Functionality
The system's specialized functionality addresses the unique needs of a major research university through components like the decentralized program finder, which enables prospective students to discover academic opportunities across the institution's diverse offerings. Faculty integration components including bio blocks, listings, and profile pages create a comprehensive directory system that showcases the university's academic talent. The news system encompasses featured news presentations, comprehensive listings, and individual post templates that support the university's extensive communications needs. Events integration through LiveWhale provides dynamic content that keeps the community informed about the institution's vibrant campus life, while flexible form integration supports multiple solutions and request-for-information capabilities essential for enrollment and engagement.

Template System
The template architecture provides a hierarchy of layouts designed to serve different communication needs across the university. The flagship template offers a unique homepage experience with specialized components that reflect Carnegie Mellon's distinctive character and achievements. Secondary templates provide flexible layouts specifically designed for college and unit landing pages, allowing individual schools to maintain their identity while adhering to university-wide design standards. Tertiary templates focus on content presentation with sidebar navigation systems that enhance user experience on deeper pages. Specialized page templates for faculty profiles, academic programs, news listings, and marketing campaigns ensure that every type of content has an optimized presentation format.

Site Type Architecture
Multi-Site Implementation Strategy
The system architecture supports three distinct site contexts through a sophisticated component availability matrix that ensures appropriate functionality while maintaining brand consistency. Components designated as "Flagship Only" include specialized elements like the homepage hero, impactful partnerships section, and faculty stats with testimonials that reflect the university's unique position and achievements. "Flagship & Unit Sites" share essential components such as news systems, events integration, and feature panels that serve both institutional communication and individual unit needs. "Unit Sites Only" components include specialized functionality like detailed faculty profiles, program finders, and academic program pages that address the specific requirements of individual schools and departments. This strategic approach ensures brand consistency across the entire university ecosystem while providing units with the autonomy to manage content that reflects their unique missions and audiences.

Key Features & Innovations
Distributed Content Management
The new architecture revolutionizes how Carnegie Mellon manages content across its extensive digital ecosystem by enabling individual units to maintain their own content while adhering to established brand standards. This distributed approach eliminates previous bottlenecks in content creation and updates, allowing schools and departments to respond quickly to their communities' needs. The centralized design system ensures visual consistency and user experience standards, while decentralized content control empowers units with the autonomy they need to serve their specific audiences effectively. Streamlined governance processes provide clear guidelines and approval workflows that maintain quality while reducing administrative overhead.

Responsive Design System
The entire system is built on a mobile-first philosophy with comprehensive breakpoint coverage that ensures optimal user experience across all devices and screen sizes. Accessibility compliance through semantic markup and thoughtful interaction design makes the university's digital resources available to all users, regardless of their abilities or the technology they use to access content. Performance optimization is built into every component, with lazy loading, optimized images, and efficient code delivery that ensures fast page loads even on slower connections.

Integration Capabilities
The platform's extensive integration capabilities reflect the complex technology ecosystem of a major research university. LiveWhale events integration provides dynamic content that automatically updates across relevant pages, keeping the community informed about campus activities and academic events. Support for multiple form solutions including Wufoo and other platforms accommodates the university's diverse needs for data collection and user engagement. The faculty directory system integration creates a comprehensive resource that connects seamlessly with existing university databases, while news and content syndication capabilities ensure that important information reaches audiences across multiple touchpoints.

Advanced Functionality
Video integration supporting YouTube, Vimeo, and Kaltura platforms provides content creators with flexibility in how they incorporate multimedia elements into their communications. Sophisticated image carousel systems with lazy loading optimize performance while creating engaging visual experiences. Interactive timeline components enable storytelling that brings the university's rich history and ongoing achievements to life. Advanced search integration connects seamlessly with the university's existing search portal, ensuring users can find information quickly and efficiently across the entire digital ecosystem.

Results & Impact
Brand Enhancement
The redesigned digital presence delivers a modern, cohesive visual identity that spans all university digital properties, creating a unified experience that reflects Carnegie Mellon's position as a leading research institution. The improved user experience features intuitive navigation and enhanced content discovery tools that help prospective students, current community members, and external stakeholders find the information they need quickly and efficiently. Enhanced mobile responsiveness ensures that the university's digital resources are accessible to users regardless of how they choose to engage, while comprehensive accessibility compliance demonstrates the institution's commitment to inclusive design.

Operational Improvements
The standardized component library has fundamentally transformed development processes, dramatically reducing the time required to deploy new sites while ensuring consistency across the university's digital ecosystem. Improved governance through clear workflow processes, comprehensive code review, and systematic approval systems has eliminated previous inefficiencies while maintaining high quality standards. Increased traffic resulting from the modern design and improved user experience demonstrates the tangible impact of strategic digital investment. The scalable architecture provides a robust foundation that supports rapid deployment of additional unit sites without requiring fundamental system changes, enabling the university to respond quickly to evolving needs.

Technical Benefits
The component-based architecture delivers significant reductions in maintenance overhead by eliminating redundant code and ensuring that updates can be deployed efficiently across multiple sites. Improved code quality through collaborative review processes between external development expertise and internal institutional knowledge creates a more robust and maintainable system. Enhanced security through Pantheon's managed hosting environment provides enterprise-level protection for sensitive university data and communications. Better performance optimization across all site instances ensures that users enjoy fast, responsive experiences that reflect positively on the institution's technological sophistication.

Ongoing Partnership Model
Continuous Collaboration
The ongoing partnership model ensures regular maintenance and feature enhancements that keep the university's digital presence current with evolving technology standards and user expectations. Collaborative development between Knectar and Carnegie Mellon's internal team creates a knowledge-sharing environment that builds institutional capacity while leveraging external expertise. Iterative improvements based on user feedback and analytics data ensure that the system continues to evolve in response to actual usage patterns and community needs.

Governance & Maintenance
Established code review processes provide quality control that maintains high standards while enabling rapid deployment of new features and content. Clear deployment pipelines from development through staging to production ensure that changes are thoroughly tested before reaching end users. Regular security updates and performance optimization maintain the system's reliability and speed, while comprehensive training and documentation for content managers across units ensure that the sophisticated tools available through the new system are used effectively.

Technical Innovation Highlights
• Component Flexibility: The system's architecture allows for sophisticated content management with components that can be enabled or disabled based on site context, providing unprecedented flexibility while maintaining consistency.
• Workflow Integration: The GitLab and Pantheon Upstream integration creates a seamless development-to-production pipeline that supports both rapid iteration and enterprise-level quality control.
• Scalable Foundation: The distributed CMS approach provides a foundation that can support dozens of additional unit sites without requiring fundamental architectural changes.

Conclusion
The Carnegie Mellon University website redesign represents a successful collaboration between design expertise, technical innovation, and strategic implementation. By creating a scalable, component-based architecture supported by modern development workflows, the project has not only modernized CMU's digital presence but established a foundation for continued growth and innovation.

The 18-month investment has yielded a system that serves immediate needs while providing the flexibility and scalability required for long-term success. The ongoing partnership model ensures continuous improvement and adaptation to evolving university needs.

Key Success Factors: The project's success stems from the collaborative approach between multiple specialized partners, each contributing essential expertise to create a solution greater than the sum of its parts. The component-based architecture enables unprecedented reusability and consistency while providing the flexibility individual units need to serve their unique audiences. Modern development workflows support both quality assurance and scalability, ensuring that the system can grow and evolve with the university's needs. Most importantly, the strategic focus on both immediate impact and long-term flexibility has created a digital foundation that will serve Carnegie Mellon's mission for years to come.

This case study demonstrates how strategic partnerships, modern technical architecture, and thoughtful implementation can transform complex institutional digital ecosystems while supporting autonomous content management and brand consistency.

Case Study: Implementing Clarkson University's Website on Pantheon

Background
In 2022 Clarkson University partnered with Carnegie (formerly mStoner) to reimagine its institutional website. Carnegie's discovery sessions identified the need to bring Clarkson's brand and story to life, prioritize user experience and accessibility, and integrate multiple systems into a single, streamlined web presence. Carnegie prepared the creative and content strategy and produced a technical blueprint for a new site built in Drupal 9. Knectar (referred to as "our team" in this case study) was engaged to implement that strategy on Pantheon.

Goals
The project's priorities were clearly defined in the technical strategy document:

• Launch a high‑performing, accessible website that meets WCAG 2.1 AA standards.

• Provide a sustainable and modern Drupal CMS so distributed editors can create flexible pages with ease.

• Consolidate subdomains and migrate existing Drupal 8 content into a single Drupal 9 site.

• Integrate with existing systems such as PeopleSoft for faculty data, EMS for events and RaveAlert for emergency notifications.

The team also needed to improve search, enable personalization using Carnegie's Clarity tool, and accommodate future enhancements.

Design and Strategy by Carnegie
Carnegie provided the creative vision and web‑governance strategy. Their discovery work captured stakeholder goals such as showcasing faculty research, making program information easier to find and creating consistent, streamlined user paths. Carnegie's design system emphasised inclusive language, representation of Clarkson's warm community, and the distinctive sense of place across its three campuses.

On the technical side, Carnegie prepared non‑proprietary front‑end code using modern tooling (PostCSS, webpack, NPM). This "from‑scratch" approach avoided bloated frameworks and produced a living style guide for Clarkson's future use. Carnegie also established a flexible Drupal architecture based on Content Types and Paragraphs, enabling editors to assemble pages from modular components such as hero banners, statistics, feature panels and testimonials. They advocated for personalization via Clarity and recommended replacing Solr with Funnelback to deliver relevant search results across Drupal and external WordPress sites.

Our Implementation on Pantheon

Infrastructure and Deployment
Our team implemented the new site on Pantheon, taking advantage of its dev/test/live workflow and automated deployment pipeline. Pantheon's container‑based architecture allowed us to implement Drupal 9 with robust caching and scalability. Git‑based version control ensured traceable updates, and we configured continuous integration to promote builds from development through staging to production. This setup reduced risk during content migration and allowed non‑technical stakeholders to preview updates before launch.

Drupal 9 Build
Using Carnegie's front‑end code and design system as a foundation, we built a custom Drupal 9 theme and a suite of content types matching the specifications document. Key templates included:

• Homepage – featuring fixed hero and testimonial components, statistic panels and a customizable feature slider.

• Full‑width pages for section landing pages and tertiary pages for general content, both allowing editors to insert paragraphs such as hero banners, testimonial quotes, feature panels, visual router grids and statistics.

• Program pages and a program finder. The program finder searched by program name and keywords and grouped related degrees into expandable drawers, a design similar to Harvard's program finder.

• Event detail pages, news/story content types and microsite templates with separate headers/footers.

Custom modules were developed to support advanced features such as Funnelback search integration, emergency alert banners and Slate/Qualtrics form embeds. We also implemented the Clarity personalization scripts and configured Google Tag Manager and CrazyEgg analytics tools as recommended.

Accessibility
Accessibility was treated as a foundational requirement. We worked closely with Carnegie's designers to ensure semantic HTML, proper heading structure and keyboard‑navigable components. Alt text fields were enforced for images, ARIA labels were added to interactive elements, and color palettes were tested for sufficient contrast. In addition, we integrated a site‑wide accessibility monitoring system (e.g., SiteImprove or DubBot) as suggested in the technical strategy. This system runs automated scans, flags issues and provides remediation guidance, complementing manual audits to ensure ongoing WCAG 2.1 AA compliance.

PeopleSoft Directory & Faculty Profiles
One of the most significant technical challenges was creating a dynamic faculty directory. Clarkson maintains its directory data in PeopleSoft and exports the information nightly into a file. Our team built a Drupal module that reads this export every morning and updates Drupal profiles accordingly. The integration populates fields such as name, title, department, email, phone, office location, mailbox and office hours. Editors can override certain fields (e.g., name or email) while fields like title and department remain authoritative.

Beyond basic contact details, faculty profiles include a Bio paragraph and additional sections like education background, experience, research interests, teaching interests, grants and publications. We implemented WYSIWYG paragraphs for these sections, giving faculty the ability to enrich their profiles. The module also records PeopleSoft overrides and headshot images, and it supports adding custom paragraphs such as accordions or tables for special content.

For public visitors, we created a faculty directory listing that queries the pool of profiles and renders them using the tertiary page template. We replicated Clarkson's interactive org chart for departments, again sourcing data from PeopleSoft. Our solution ensures that faculty data stays current while giving Clarkson control over editorial content. We continue to provide ongoing import and cleanup support, monitoring nightly imports, resolving data anomalies and coordinating with Clarkson's IT team to adjust field mappings as PeopleSoft changes.

Search, Events and Other Integrations

Search: We configured Funnelback to index both the Drupal site and external WordPress sites (e.g., announcements.clarkson.edu), delivering unified search results that are styled to match the new design.

Calendar: The specification recommended using Clarkson's EMS calendar as the master source for events. We set up RSS imports to display upcoming events on key landing pages and built an optional integration to pull EMS data directly into Drupal for a seamless experience.

Forms and Chat: The site continues to use a combination of Slate and Drupal webforms; our team styled sample forms per the design and ensured that embedded Slate forms post directly to Slate while Drupal webforms store submissions locally. We configured the Unibuddy/Slate chat widgets and emergency alert banner so editors can toggle them as needed.

Microsites: We implemented functionality for microsite sections with distinct headers, footers and navigation sets. These sub‑sites live within the main Drupal installation but can present unique branding while still leveraging the shared design system.

Migration and Training
Migrating content from the legacy Drupal 8 site required careful planning. We built migration scripts to map old content types to the new structure, preserving metadata and redirecting URLs. Two types of redirects—server‑level patterns and page‑level rules—were implemented to handle the change in URL schema. After launch, we conducted training sessions for Clarkson's distributed editors, demonstrating how to assemble pages using paragraphs, manage the directory overrides and use Funnelback search reporting to refine content.

Impact
The new clarkson.edu site launched on Pantheon with a modern, flexible architecture and fully responsive design. Key outcomes include:

• Accessibility compliance: The site meets WCAG 2.1 AA standards and continues to be monitored through automated tools.

• Improved search and navigation: Funnelback provides comprehensive results, and the program finder makes it easy to explore academic offerings.

• Unified faculty directory: Nightly PeopleSoft imports ensure accurate faculty data while allowing rich, editable biographies.

• Enhanced user experience: Modular templates and personalization capabilities create engaging pathways for prospective students and other audiences.

• Sustainable CMS: Editors across campus can build pages without developer assistance, and Pantheon's workflow enables safe updates and continuous improvement.

Conclusion
Clarkson University's website redesign is a prime example of effective collaboration. Carnegie Higher Ed provided the strategic vision, brand positioning and design system, while our team executed the technical implementation on Pantheon, ensuring accessibility, system integrations and long‑term maintainability. By integrating PeopleSoft data, enabling personalization and building a flexible Drupal 9 foundation, we delivered a site that meets Clarkson's goals today and can evolve with the university's needs.

Yale Center for British Art – Digital Transformation on Pantheon

Background and project goals
The Yale Center for British Art (YCBA) is a leading art museum whose digital presence must support exhibitions, programs, scholarly research and access to a collection of more than 2,000 paintings, 250 sculptures, ~20,000 drawings and watercolors, 40,000 prints, 35,000 rare books and manuscripts, and an additional reference library of 40,000 volumes.

Prior to 2019 the YCBA operated a large Drupal‑7 site for the museum and a separate BlackLight‑based Ruby on Rails application for its collections search. Knectar and design partner Fabrique were engaged to design and implement a modern digital platform that would unify the visitor experience while meeting strict accessibility and technical requirements. Key goals included:

• Modern platform & UX. Replace the aging web properties with Drupal 10/11 websites on Pantheon that match Fabrique's modern designs and provide an intuitive experience across devices.

• Search & discoverability. Provide robust search across exhibitions, events and the collection. The museum site uses Drupal's built‑in search with result weighting for keywords, sticky/promoted content and recency. The collections site implements a headless search front‑end backed by Apache Solr, giving visitors facets such as collection, creator, date range, on‑site access, image use and classification.

• Accessibility & compliance. Comply with WCAG 2.0 Level AA, following Yale's web‑accessibility checklist and implementing editorial workflows for content review.

• Scalability & maintainability. Host on Pantheon's managed infrastructure for stability and ease of deployment, utilise reusable modules and contribute Solr integration code back to the Drupal community.

Project partners and responsibilities

Partner
Role
Key contributions

Fabrique
Design & UX strategy
Created the visual/UX design system, navigation structures and static templates used to guide the build (e.g., static site prototypes and template matrix).

Knectar
Implementation partner
Led Drupal development, architected Pantheon environments, implemented custom modules, carried out accessibility compliance and integrated external services.

YCBA & Yale ITS
Stakeholders
Provided content expertise, managed domains & DNS, validated accessibility and technical compliance.

Main museum website (Drupal 10 on Pantheon)

Content architecture & navigation
Fabrique's design emphasised clear navigation with dedicated channels for Exhibitions & programs, Collections, Research & learning, Plan your visit and About us. The Drupal build implements:

• Custom content types & taxonomies. The technical specification defines multiple content types (Events, Exhibitions, Generic content, People, Story) and taxonomies such as Event Type, Tag, Page Type and People Type. These allow site editors to structure and filter content intuitively.

• Dynamic navigation. Menu items can display thumbnails, event types, titles, dates and teaser text. For example, the "What's on" menu automatically lists the two most recent exhibition nodes unless overridden by a "Sticky at top of lists" flag.

• Flexible page templates. Templates cover the homepage, event and exhibition overviews, past events, stories, press listings, people profiles and search results. Each includes fielded content (title, hero image, featured sections, video blocks, etc.), enabling editors to populate layouts without developer assistance.

Search & SEO
Drupal search with weighting. At launch the site uses Drupal's standard search, with weightings for keyword relevance, sticky/promoted content and recency. Results pages show the query, number of results, filter options (relevance or newest first) and a link to the collections search.

SEO enhancements. Knectar implemented the Real‑time SEO for Drupal module (Yoast replacement) and Simple Sitemap to automatically generate XML sitemaps and handle meta tags. Google Analytics integration and meta‑data support allow better marketing insight.

Third‑party integrations & features

• Bedework feed for events. Event data is exported to a feed consumed by Yale's Bedework calendar.

• Google Tag Manager & analytics. GTM code is embedded for analytics and marketing.

• YouTube video support. Video blocks embed videos hosted on YouTube.

• Google Places API to display real‑time opening hours on the homepage.

• CAS (Central Authentication Service) for single sign‑on (SSO) for internal editors.

• Mandrill for transactional email handling.

Editorial workflow & user roles
The site defines user roles (Super‑admin, Admin, Editor, Author) and uses the Workflows module to support a structured editorial process: save draft, content review, approval, publish and unpublish. This process ensures content quality and accessibility compliance before publication.

Accessibility & compliance
YCBA required compliance with WCAG 2.0 Level AA; the technical specification references Yale's accessibility checklist. Knectar implemented accessible navigation, semantic HTML and ARIA roles, ensured proper contrast ratios, and tested with screen readers. A similar process applies to the new collections site (see below).

Infrastructure
Pantheon hosting. The site is hosted on Pantheon under Yale's account with SSL enabled by default. Knectar configured Dev/Test/Live environments and Git‑based deployment workflows.

Modules & tooling. Additional modules include Redirect (bulk redirect management), Focal Point (image handling), Mandrill (email), XML Sitemap and Metatags.

Collections search (headless Drupal 11 on Pantheon)

Motivation and data sources
The existing BlackLight Ruby on Rails application served as the collections search, indexing object metadata, artist metadata and library holdings in a Solr schema. The aim of the new project is to bring this functionality into a modern, headless Drupal environment while preserving the features that researchers rely on. The collections hold more than 56,000 prints and drawings, 39,000 library items, 21,000 rare books and manuscripts and thousands of other works.

Architecture
Headless Drupal 11. The collections search is implemented as a decoupled front‑end (Nuxt/Next‑style) that communicates with Drupal via APIs. Drupal acts as an API and configuration backend while Solr remains the authoritative search index.

Remote Solr integration module. Knectar built a custom module to query an authenticated Solr instance. The specification describes using dynamic fields (e.g., *_ss, *_txt, *_i) and copyfields for date and geo facets. Query configuration (facets, fields, boost queries) mirrors the former BlackLight setup. Generalizing this module as a contributed project delivers reusability, extensibility and community collaboration.

Faceted search UI. Visitors can filter by collection, creator, date range, on‑site access, image use, image availability, classification and other fields. Results support pagination, sorting (e.g., by date or title), multiple view modes (tile/masonry or list) and an accessible IIIF viewer for object images.

Headless artist pages & new content types. Phase Ib introduces artist facets on landing and results pages and dedicated artist pages with metadata similar to object records. Future phases will support story/essay pages with IIIF images and align the collections landing page with the main museum homepage.

Migration phases
The collections project is staged:

• Phase I (through March 2025). Technical discovery, analysis of legacy code and BlackLight search logic; creation of Pantheon environments; development of new custom Drupal theme; implementation of remote Solr API integration and query modules; basic accessibility and performance testing. After content review and ADA compliance testing, a soft launch will publish the collections data via Drupal while retaining the existing design.

• Phase Ib. Full transition of data and functionality to Drupal 10/11. Deliverables include implementing the high‑level architecture (object, artist and library metadata), replicating all BlackLight views (landing page, search results, object records) and adding new artist facets and pages. URL parameters such as search field, pagination, sorting and view modes must be preserved to maintain deep linking.

• Phase II (design update). From January 2025, Fabrique will provide redesigned templates. Knectar will update the Drupal themes, refine query logic for artist lists, and support story content. The redesigned site is expected to publish by June 2025.

Compliance and testing
Each phase includes UI testing across supported browsers, accessibility testing (WCAG Levels 1 and 2), technical infrastructure compliance, performance and load testing, disaster recovery and operational compliance. The site will undergo review by Yale's ITS Accessibility team before launch.

Impact and results

• Unified digital experience. Visitors now experience a coherent design language across the main museum site and collections search, with intuitive navigation and clear calls to search the collection.

• Enhanced discoverability. The new sites provide multiple entry points for exploration, from exhibitions and events on the museum site to powerful faceted search across the collection (including 56k+ works on paper, 39k library items and 21k rare books).

• Accessibility leadership. Implementing WCAG 2.0 Level AA compliance ensures the site is usable by people with disabilities. The case study emphasises physical and digital accessibility, including accessible navigation, contrast ratios and screen‑reader testing.

• Performance & maintainability. Hosting on Pantheon and using modern Drupal ensures scalable performance, streamlined deployments and security. The remote Solr integration decouples the search backend for flexibility and caching.

• Community contribution. Knectar's Solr module is designed for generalisation and contribution back to the Drupal community, enabling other institutions to leverage remote Solr search.

Conclusion
The Yale Center for British Art's digital transformation demonstrates how a heritage institution can modernise its web presence while honouring accessibility and scholarly requirements. By partnering with Fabrique for design and Knectar for technical execution, the YCBA successfully launched a Drupal 10 museum site and is nearing completion of a headless Drupal 11 collections search backed by Apache Solr. The project showcases best practices in modular content architecture, faceted search, accessibility compliance and open‑source contribution, positioning the YCBA for future growth and engagement.

Case Study: Fox Chase Cancer Center Website Redesign and Implementation (2015–2016)

Background
Fox Chase Cancer Center (FCCC) in Philadelphia is a world‑renowned National Cancer Institute–designated comprehensive cancer center. By 2015 the center's website had grown organically for years and was not meeting the needs of modern audiences. Patients needed clear navigation to clinical services and appointment requests, researchers wanted to highlight scientific programs, and the institution's marketing team wanted flexible storytelling tools. FCCC hired Transit Authority Figures (Rob & Damia) to provide design and user‑experience strategy and partnered with Knectar to implement the new site in Drupal.

Objectives and Challenges

• Simplify navigation for patients, visitors, scientists and donors. FCCC has dozens of departments, research programs and patient resources. The goal was to make this content easy to find and interrelate.

• Enable flexible storytelling without breaking the design. Content administrators needed the ability to assemble pages with slideshows, pull quotes, related stories and lists without calling developers.

• Provide powerful search tools. The site needed intuitive search for doctors and scientists and a way to query clinical trials and programs. External tools such as Google Search Appliance had to be integrated.

• Ensure accessibility and responsiveness. FCCC required compliance with Temple University's accessibility guidelines; text must be resizable up to 200 %, images needed alternative text and the site had to work on phones, tablets and desktops.

• Integrate with third‑party services. Video hosting, maps, event calendars and forms were hosted off site and needed to be embedded cleanly.

Collaboration and Approach

Design & Strategy: Transit Authority Figures
Rob & Damia from Transit Authority Figures developed the site's information architecture and visual design. They created page templates for the home page, news/events/blog listings and inner pages. These layouts used a flexible grid with generous white space, muted typography and photography featuring clinicians and patients. The designs included features such as:

• A prominent hero slideshow on the home page with captions and call‑to‑action buttons.

• Modular components for news, events and blog posts that could be combined in one or three columns.

• Pull‑quote boxes and feature story cards (seen in the design comps and interior page screenshots) to support storytelling.

• Left‑side navigation for program pages, and global secondary navigation for research and education sections to guide users.

Technical Implementation: Knectar
Knectar handled all aspects of the build, accessibility compliance and integrations. The site was implemented on Drupal and hosted on Acquia. Key technical decisions included:

• Drupal Paragraphs and NodeEmbed modules – To empower content editors, Knectar built pages using the Paragraphs module. Editors could select from predefined paragraph types (text blocks, pull quotes, slideshows, lists or WYSIWYG areas) and arrange them in any order. Slideshows were built once and embedded anywhere using NodeEmbed.

• Reusable slideshows, responsive tables and iFrames – The system allowed administrators to insert slideshows, tabbed content, tables and iFrames (e.g., clinical‑trial search forms) with consistent styling knectar.com.

• Find‑a‑Doctor and Find‑a‑Scientist search – Knectar implemented custom search interfaces using Drupal views. Users can search by name, browse by initial letter and filter by specialty, department or language. The search form auto‑scrolls to results on mobile devices.

• Google Search Appliance integration – The site search uses Google Search Appliance, allowing queries to index FCCC content and related Temple University sites knectar.com.

• Workflows and moderation – Workbench modules provide draft and publish workflows so content editors can submit changes for review without publishing.

• Accessibility features – Knectar followed Temple's ADA guidelines: relative font sizes, scalable text, alt‑text fields for images, print‑friendly pages and keyboard‑accessible navigation. A text‑size control and a "Print / Share This Page" utility appear on every page (visible in the interior screenshot).

• Third‑party embedding – Videos are served through YouTube, maps via Google Maps and external forms/clinical trials are embedded through iFrames. The chosen jReject plugin warns visitors using unsupported browsers.

Integrations and Launch
Knectar collaborated closely with Transit Authority Figures and Temple University to translate the approved designs into mobile‑responsive Drupal themes. Knectar's developers created custom content types for news, events, blog posts, clinical trials and patient stories. The site uses the Focal Point module to ensure images display important subjects within different aspect ratios. A global block‑placement tool allows editors to add call‑to‑action blocks or related content to any page. The site launched in late 2015 after an iterative QA process and content migration.

Outcomes

Case Study: Implementing Kettering University's Website

Project overview
Kettering University undertook a comprehensive redesign and rebuild of its public‑facing website to align the institution's digital presence with its modern academic priorities and co‑op‑based learning model. Carnegie Higher Ed served as the design and strategy partner, developing the site's information architecture, user‑experience patterns and visual direction. Knectar executed the implementation—upgrading the Drupal CMS, building custom templates and components, migrating content, integrating external data sources and ensuring accessibility compliance.

Goals

• Modernize the platform – Upgrade Kettering University's Drupal installation to Drupal 10 and replace legacy templates and paragraphs with a component‑based system.

• Reflect the university's priorities – Build templates that showcase academic programs, experiential co‑op education and research while supporting the institution's shift toward advanced mobility, new energy vehicles, intelligent manufacturing, artificial intelligence and sustainability.

• Improve usability and accessibility – Consolidate content types, adopt a consistent design language and implement accessible markup so that visitors (including those with disabilities) can easily navigate and consume content.

• Integrate data sources – Connect the website to external systems for program data, events, news, social media and faculty profiles.

• Enable phased roll‑out – Adopt an incremental implementation strategy that allows the university to review each release, conduct quality assurance and train content owners before the next phase begins.

Implementation strategy
Carnegie Higher Ed provided a detailed implementation strategy that guided the project timeline. The strategy broke the work into four phases, beginning with pre‑phase activities and culminating in optional enhancements if budget allowed.

Pre‑phase and Phase 1 – foundation

• Component inventory and planning – Before development began, Kettering reviewed and approved the inventory of components to be built. Unused paragraphs from the legacy site were pared down to reduce bloat.

• Global theme updates – The first phase focused on updating the global theme and style system based on the Carnegie design. This baseline allowed new components to inherit the updated visual language.

• Legacy template review – The team performed quality assurance on legacy templates to ensure that the new theme did not introduce regression issues. Content managers were involved to validate that theming changes preserved content integrity.

• Stakeholder socialization – Kettering collaborated with Carnegie to plan the internal roll‑out of the new information architecture and global styles.

Phase 2 – new templates and program finder
Phase 2 ran from March to mid‑June. Key deliverables included:

• Program detail template – A new content type ("Program Detail") was fielded to support program pages and the program finder. Each program includes dedicated fields (e.g., program name, college, department, contact email and phone) and a "Contact Admissions" block that can vary by program. The schema is based on the tertiary layout.

• Homepage and program finder – The new homepage and associated paragraphs were created. The program finder is a stand‑alone view that provides a filterable list of programs. This view was integrated into the homepage and program pages.

• Academic program page – New paragraphs were built for program landing pages, including hero sections, stats panels, feature panels and calls‑to‑action.

• No content freeze – Content editing could continue on the existing site during development; final reconciliation occurred at the end of the phase.

Phase 3 – audience gateways and admissions
Phase 3 ran from June to July. Deliverables included:

• Audience gateway ("Student One‑Stop") – A large umbrella page designed to consolidate key resources for students; this required a content freeze or syncing process due to the breadth of content.

• Admissions & Aid page – A template for admissions content, aligning design patterns with other major pages.

• Menu structure alignment – Developers provided an environment for stakeholders to review and socialize the new navigation/IA structure.

• Campus socialization – Kettering managed stakeholder communication and migration planning.

Phase 4 – optional enhancements
The final phase (July–August) included optional work if budget allowed:

• Additional templates – A card view for the program finder and templates for the admissions blog landing and post pages.

• Course catalog integration – Carnegie estimated 20–30 hours to build an integration with the course catalog (not including design work).

• Content reconciliation – A slower content editing pace followed by a final reconciliation at the end of the phase.

Technical implementation by Knectar
While Carnegie provided design and strategy, Knectar executed the technical implementation. The work spanned a large Drupal upgrade, custom theming, paragraph and view development, integrations and accessibility compliance.

Drupal 10 upgrade and content architecture
Kettering's legacy site used a collection of templates and paragraphs that had accumulated over time. Knectar upgraded the site to Drupal 10 and built a component‑based system. Templates correspond to common page types—Home, Secondary, Tertiary, Tertiary‑Minimal, Admissions, Co‑Op, Program, News Detail, Event Detail, Faculty Detail, Program Finder, Faculty Directory and Department Landing. For each template, corresponding paragraph components were created. The project documentation lists global components such as Hero, Stats Panel, Latest News, Featured Events, Instagram Feed, CTA Panel, Intro Text block and various multi‑column panels. These reusable components enable content editors to build diverse layouts while maintaining consistency.

Program and course integration
The Program Detail content type provides a structured schema for academic programs. It includes fields for the program name, associated college and department, contact information and a program‑specific admissions call‑to‑action. Knectar mapped data from existing program pages into this schema and implemented the Program Finder view to display programs in a filterable list.

News and events
Knectar created News Detail and Event Detail content types to support list views. The news schema includes fields for title, date, tags, image, teaser and body. The event schema includes fields such as title, subtitle, taxonomy tag, date, time range, ticket information, location, registration link, body, image and caption. These fields allow content editors to manage events and news articles while automatically generating lists and featured panels.

Faculty schema import and directory
One of the critical integrations was the Faculty Detail schema. The documentation notes that this content type is "fielded specifically to support Faculty List views and/or the Directory" and is based on the tertiary layout. Knectar implemented a Faculty Directory view that displays faculty in a filterable list.

Because faculty profiles already existed in external systems, Knectar built an import routine to map faculty data—name, title, department, contact information and biography—into the new Faculty Detail content type. The mapping ensured that the site could automatically update faculty profiles when data changed in the source system. The directory view uses exposed filters (e.g., by department or keyword) and links each listing to a full profile page, maintaining search‑engine‑friendly URLs and rich schema markup.

Social media and third‑party integrations

• Instagram feed – The global "Instagram Feed" component embeds a photo carousel labeled "Connect with #ketteringuniversity," using custom HTML with an API link and Juicer integration.

• CTA panels and visual router – Several components provide calls‑to‑action and image grids, empowering editors to highlight priority content.

• Forms and Slate – The project includes templates for form pages that integrate with Kettering's Slate system to handle requests for information and other inquiry forms.

• Future course catalog integration – As an optional enhancement, the team considered integrating the course catalog to surface course data directly on program pages.

Accessibility and quality assurance
Knectar ensured that all new components conformed to WCAG guidelines. Templates use semantic HTML, ARIA attributes and proper heading hierarchies. Components such as heroes, stats panels and visual router grids were designed to be navigable by screen readers and accessible via keyboard. Knectar also implemented alt‑text fields on images and provided editors with guidance on writing meaningful descriptions. QA rounds in each phase included cross‑browser testing and accessibility checks to verify compliance.

Outcomes and impact

• Modernized, flexible site – The Drupal 10 upgrade and component‑based architecture provide Kettering with a modern, maintainable platform. Editors can assemble pages from reusable paragraphs while maintaining brand consistency.

• Enhanced user experience – The new site highlights Kettering's academic strengths and unique co‑op program through well‑structured templates and dynamic lists (e.g., program finder, news and events, faculty directory). Clear navigation and consistent design improve the visitor journey.

• Integrated data and automation – The implementation connects external data sources—program data, faculty profiles, social media and Slate forms—reducing manual data entry and ensuring up‑to‑date information. The faculty schema import and program finder are examples of this automation.

• Accessibility compliance – By prioritizing accessible markup and testing, the new site provides an inclusive experience for users with disabilities and positions Kettering favorably for ADA compliance.

• Collaborative phased approach – The four‑phase strategy allowed Kettering to review each release, perform quality assurance and manage content reconciliation without disrupting operations. The collaborative process ensured that the design vision provided by Carnegie Higher Ed was faithfully implemented by Knectar.

Conclusion
Kettering University's website project demonstrates how a collaborative partnership between a design/strategy firm and a technical implementation team can produce a modern, accessible and data‑driven digital experience. Carnegie Higher Ed's research and design insights shaped the site's information architecture and visual language, while Knectar's technical expertise brought the vision to life through a Drupal 10 upgrade, component‑based templates, custom integrations and rigorous accessibility testing. The result is a scalable, user‑friendly website that reflects Kettering's innovative spirit and supports prospective students, current students, faculty and alumni alike.

Case study: Knectar implementation of the Lewis Katz School of Medicine website

Project context and goals
Temple University's Lewis Katz School of Medicine (LKSOM) wanted to modernize its public‑facing website to better communicate its academic programs, research achievements and community outreach. The existing site offered limited flexibility for content administrators, lacked a unified visual identity and did not meet accessibility standards. Temple engaged Transit Authority Figures (TAF) – designers Rob and Damia – to create a bold design and information‑architecture strategy, and partnered with Knectar to build the site on Drupal. The project delivered:

  • • A new homepage built around a dynamic slideshow and clear calls‑to‑action. Specifications called for a slideshow that could become static when only one slide was enabled, with fields for an image, headline, caption, caption positioning and destination URL. Administrators also needed a Quick Links field and a block‑placer so they could assemble homepage components.
  • • Flexible inner pages that allowed content editors to assemble body copy, slideshows and related story blocks. NodeEmbed was used so editors could embed slideshows within page bodies without writing code.
  • • A searchable faculty directory. Users can search by name, browse alphabetically or filter by research centre, basic science department or clinical department. Predictive search suggests names as the user types and clicking a suggestion takes them directly to the person's profile.
  • • A modular content‑management system using Workbench modules. Roles – Root, Developer, Site Admin, Content Admin and Content Editor – control permissions; content editors can create or edit pages but cannot publish them without approval.

From the outset, accessibility was a core requirement. Temple University's Web Accessibility Standards specified that all fonts use relative sizes and that text must be resizable up to 200 percent without loss of content. The site also needed alt‑text fields for every image and compliance testing using Temple's internal tools or public ADA scanners. Knectar was responsible for meeting these standards during implementation.

Partnership and roles
The project was a three‑way collaboration:

  • • Transit Authority Figures (Rob and Damia) – Led design and user‑experience strategy. Their research and design work resulted in a vibrant, image‑rich layout that highlights the school's mission and programs. The homepage design uses large visuals and typography to draw attention to strategic messaging.
  • • Temple University web team – Provided content, approved designs and assisted with institutional integrations such as Google Custom Search and the university events feed.
  • • Knectar – Implemented the site on Drupal, built custom modules, implemented accessibility features, integrated third‑party systems and performed quality assurance. Knectar also coordinated with Temple IT on hosting and deployment.

Implementation highlights

Translating design into a responsive Drupal theme
Knectar built a responsive Drupal theme based on TAF's designs. The homepage slideshow models the smooth left‑to‑right transition used by Stanford Medicine and includes pagination dots, headlines and captions. When only one slide is published, the slideshow becomes a static hero image, allowing the homepage to retain its impact without unnecessary animation. A Quick Links module provides persistent links to high‑traffic destinations, and a block placer lets administrators assemble rows of news, events and posts. Knectar used the Paragraphs module for complex layouts, giving editors control over text, images and calls‑to‑action.

Flexible content types and workflows
The site defines custom content types for news, events, blogs, faculty profiles and static pages. Each content type has fields for titles, summaries, body content and media. News nodes include a "push to" option that determines whether the story appears on the homepage or related‑stories blocks. A scheduler module allows editors to set future publish dates. The Workbench suite provides drafting and moderation workflows so that editors can save content and submit it for publication without having direct publishing rights. Revision capturing and the Diff module enable version comparisons and rollback.

Faculty search and directories
Knectar implemented a sophisticated faculty directory. The list page includes breadcrumbs, print and text‑size controls and ShareThis buttons. Users can search by name, browse alphabetically or filter by research centre, basic science or clinical department. Predictive search suggests names as users type and takes them directly to the corresponding profile when selected. Detail pages include a profile photo, contact information, tabbed content ("About me," "Education, Training & Credentials," "Publications") and related content blocks. Temple's editors can assemble faculty lists using Paragraphs, mixing people entries and rich‑text segments in any order.

Accessibility compliance
To meet Temple's accessibility guidelines, Knectar implemented several measures:

  • • Relative font sizes and text resizing – All typography is specified in relative units so that visitors can enlarge text up to 200 % without losing content or functionality.
  • • Alt‑text for images – Image fields include an enabled alt‑text field so editors are prompted to describe every image.
  • • Color and contrast – The design's red and white palette was tested to ensure sufficient contrast for users with low vision. Call‑to‑action buttons have clear focus states and the site works with keyboard navigation.
  • • Accessible navigation and forms – Menus and form fields are built semantically using Drupal's markup and ARIA attributes. A print‑friendly view strips extraneous styling and provides a simplified layout.

Knectar coordinated with Temple's accessibility office to run automated and manual scans, addressing issues highlighted by tools like Cynthia Says.

Third‑party integrations
Knectar integrated several external services:

  • • Events feed – The site pulls an XML feed from Temple's events calendar (events.temple.edu) to populate an events block. Department pages automatically filter events based on matching tags.
  • • Google Analytics and ShareThis – Standard Drupal modules integrate analytics tracking and social‑sharing buttons. ShareThis appears on inner pages, news and blog posts, enabling visitors to share content easily.
  • • jReject and Chosen – jReject notifies users of unsupported browsers, while the Chosen JavaScript plugin enhances select menus with search and improved accessibility.
  • • Google Custom Search – Site search results are powered by Google Custom Search and styled to match the site's look and feel.

Outcome and impact
The new LKSOM website launched with a modern look and improved user experience. The homepage features a prominent hero message, "Do More Good," set over photos of students and faculty medicine.temple.edu. Below the hero area, visitors encounter the school's vision statement—"We will inspire a new standard of excellence in education and research and lead social change in medicine"—paired with quick links to programs such as the MD Program, Physician Assistant Program, Graduate Medical Education and the Health Justice and Bioethics Program medicine.temple.edu. News items and community spotlights call attention to research awards and outreach activities; for example, a featured story notes that Katz welcomed local high‑school students for a hands‑on Health Careers Exploration Day medicine.temple.edu.

The new site improves content management for Temple's communications team. Editors can create pages, news, events and faculty profiles using standardized forms and easily rearrange components through the block‑placer. The predictive faculty search and filter system make it simple for prospective students and researchers to find faculty by name or department. Integrations with the events feed and social‑sharing tools ensure that content remains fresh and widely disseminated.

Finally, the project demonstrates the value of collaboration between design, development and institutional stakeholders. TAF's strategic design vision, combined with Knectar's implementation expertise and Temple's content leadership, produced a site that communicates the school's mission, fosters engagement and meets rigorous accessibility and technical standards.

LIM College Website Refresh — Case Study

Background
LIM College is a private institution in New York City focused on the business of fashion. In 2023 the college decided to refresh its public‐facing website. The existing site ran on Drupal 9 and contained an extensive body of program information, admissions and financial‑aid content, news stories and landing pages. To improve the user experience and modernize the brand without starting from scratch, LIM engaged Carnegie Higher Ed to develop the creative strategy and Knectar to implement the redesign. The guiding principle was to keep as much of the existing Drupal implementation and content intact as possible while applying an updated look and feel. This approach preserved the college's investment in content and infrastructure, kept the project within budget and minimized disruption for content editors.

Project objectives and creative strategy

Goals from Carnegie's assessment
During discovery sessions with LIM, Carnegie identified key problems with the legacy site: the navigation structure was confusing, program pages did not answer prospective students' questions and calls‑to‑action were buried. The creative strategy therefore set the following goals:

  • • Refine information architecture and navigation. Carnegie recommended removing the "Online Learning" link from the primary navigation, creating dedicated pages for online programs and renaming Internships+ to Careers & Internships. They also advised clarifying the relationship between Admissions & Aid and Apply to LIM so that the former served as a high‑level overview and the latter focused on the application process.
  • • Develop a dynamic homepage. Content models proposed by Carnegie stressed the need for an immersive homepage that introduces LIM's brand message, displays a program finder, showcases student success stories, highlights key statistics and promotes calls to action such as Request Info, Visit and Apply.
  • • Create persuasive program pages and a program finder. Carnegie's wireframes defined separate templates for a program finder and academic program pages. The program finder allows users to search programs by degree level, modality (on‑campus or online), area of study and career field, then presents results in a streamlined list with calls to action. The program page content model includes a snapshot with a Request for Information (RFI) form, sections on what students will learn and career outcomes, faculty profiles, alumni/student spotlights, optional student work galleries and related programs.
  • • Simplify enrollment messaging. The content priorities call for clear, intuitive instructions that streamline enrollment and help prospects progress through the funnel.
  • • Support multilingual audiences. Analytics showed that non‑English sessions were a small but meaningful segment of site traffic and concentrated on admissions, academics and visit pages. Carnegie recommended piloting overview pages in Mandarin and Spanish that summarize admissions, cost, aid and program information.
  • • Project‑to‑process mindset. Carnegie's plan envisioned the refresh as the beginning of an ongoing improvement cycle. Continuous enhancements—through usability testing, analytics‑informed refinements and incremental functionality—would help LIM keep its content relevant and extend the life of the site.

Design system and writing plan
The creative strategy updated LIM's design system and defined a writing plan. New or refreshed components included two‑ and three‑column callouts, faculty feeds, image and video carousels, stat panels, testimonial panels, a social‑media feed, an embedded RFI form and an NYC gallery. Carnegie identified which top‑level pages, new pages (e.g., Undergraduate Degrees, Graduate Degrees, Online Degrees) and program pages would be rewritten. Key project metrics were established for user experience, design, functionality and content—including increasing traffic to admissions and online program pages, improving mobile performance and site search, and rewriting program pages to emphasize career outcomes.

Implementation approach — Knectar

Leveraging existing infrastructure
Knectar was tasked with translating Carnegie's creative vision into a functional site without rebuilding the entire platform. Our technical assessment recommended applying the new design to the existing Drupal 9 implementation rather than building a completely new front‑end. The legacy front‑end already used a modern build pipeline with a style‑guide library; by keeping class names consistent and modifying styles, Carnegie's front‑end developers could update the look without altering markup. Only pages that were entirely redesigned—such as the homepage—required new markup and twig templates.

We also evaluated which content types needed modification. Most existing content types could be retained, but the homepage and degree (program) templates required significant restructuring, and the event content type (powered by a proprietary Zensource module) would need to be replaced. The new program pages and program finder would therefore become custom templates within Drupal. Given that the Zensource modules also provided the legacy events calendar and editing theme, we planned to rebuild those functions and replace the analytics dashboard with a standard solution such as Google Analytics.

Building new templates and components
Working closely with Carnegie's wireframes, Knectar built three primary templates:

  • • Homepage template. We created a flexible Drupal content type for the homepage that integrates Carnegie's components: a hero banner for the brand message; a program finder block; a video testimonial gallery (Learn by Doing); an animated stats panel (Record that Speaks for Itself); an NYC photo gallery; an Instagram feed and a call‑to‑action panel. The template allows editors to assemble these sections using paragraph components, ensuring the page is dynamic yet easy to maintain.
  • • Program finder. The program finder uses a custom Drupal view combined with filters for degree level, modality, area of study and career field, matching Carnegie's specifications. Results are loaded asynchronously for performance and present program titles, areas of study and career paths. Each result links to its program page and includes contextual calls to action such as Request Info and Apply.
  • • Program page template. We replaced the legacy degree content type with a new program content type. Fields capture program snapshots, learning outcomes, career outcomes, faculty, alumni spotlights, student work galleries, featured courses and related programs. An embedded RFI form appears near the top, allowing visitors to request information without leaving the page. We migrated existing degree data into the new content type to maintain search‑engine rankings and continuity.

Updating the design system in Drupal
To support Carnegie's refreshed design system, Knectar implemented new and updated components as Drupal paragraph types. For example, two‑ and three‑column callouts, faculty feeds and image/video carousels were re‑implemented with accessible markup. The stat panel replaced the older accolade/stat slider component, which the component inventory had identified for replacement. Similarly, we removed the old Spotlight component and replaced tabbed interfaces with accordions to address accessibility issues. The new components use modern CSS and follow WCAG 2.1 guidelines for contrast and keyboard navigation.

Global elements such as the header, navigation and footer were re‑themed to match Carnegie's typography and color palette. Navigation labels were updated (e.g., Careers & Internships) and the application and request‑information links were emphasized, reflecting Carnegie's information‑architecture recommendations. A responsive navigation menu and optimized mobile layouts improved the mobile experience, addressing the high share of mobile sessions noted in the baseline analytics.

Integrations and accessibility
Because LIM's enrollment process relies on lead generation, integrating RFI forms was critical. The embedded RFI component submits data directly to the college's existing CRM, enabling admissions staff to follow up with prospects. We configured the forms to respect privacy regulations and provided clear consent messaging. Search‑engine optimization was improved by implementing semantic HTML, schema.org markup on program pages, and a more robust site search backed by Drupal's search API.

Accessibility compliance was a priority throughout the implementation. In addition to replacing tabbed components with accordions, we audited all templates against WCAG 2.1 Level AA standards. Images include meaningful alternative text, carousels provide play/pause controls and ARIA labels, and navigation can be used entirely with a keyboard. Color palettes were tested for contrast, and the site supports high‑contrast mode and screen‑reader landmarks.

Outcomes and impact
The redesigned LIM College website launched as a collaborative effort between Carnegie Higher Ed's strategic design and Knectar's technical implementation. Key achievements include:

  • • Improved navigation and information architecture. The top‑level navigation now clearly differentiates academics, admissions, student life, careers & internships, and about sections, with dedicated pages for online and graduate programs.
  • • Dynamic homepage and program finder. Prospective students can quickly explore programs through the homepage program finder and filter options by degree level, modality, area of study and career field.
  • • Robust program pages. Each program page combines program overviews, career outcomes, faculty profiles and alumni stories, supported by embedded RFI forms. These pages help LIM articulate the value of its programs and encourage inquiries.
  • • Updated design system. New components—stat panels, carousels, testimonial panels, call‑to‑action panels and social media feeds—deliver an engaging experience while keeping the underlying Drupal structure intact.
  • • Accessibility and mobile performance. Replacing the old tab components with accordions, ensuring proper semantics and optimizing layouts for mobile devices have made the site more inclusive. Baseline analytics showed that 48 % of sessions occurred on mobile and that mobile visitors had shorter sessions; the new design directly addresses these issues.
  • • Foundation for continuous improvement. By preserving the Drupal architecture and implementing Carnegie's process‑oriented strategy, the project sets the stage for ongoing enhancements. Editors can manage content with familiar paragraph and layout tools, and the site can evolve with additional components or A/B‑tested changes without a wholesale rebuild.

Acknowledgements
This case study highlights a successful collaboration between Carnegie Higher Ed and Knectar. Carnegie created the information‑architecture recommendations, content models, wireframes and writing plan that informed the redesign. Knectar implemented the project in Drupal 9, including new templates, a program finder, refreshed components, accessibility compliance and integrations. Together, these efforts produced a modern, user‑centered website that reflects LIM College's brand and supports its recruitment goals.

Automated emails notify users and admins when badge types change, reducing help‑desk loops. Throughout, we used Drupal's Layout Builder to keep the interface responsive and accessible; non‑admin members see a streamlined dashboard with events, training, and badge status, while administrators get deeper views for users, events, and companies. Carv.io – From time sheets to true capacity forecasting

Carv.io was born from a simple question most small and mid‑sized teams can't answer with their current tools: Are we staffed for the work that's really coming? Time trackers, ticket boards, and static resource calendars are good at recording the past and organizing the present, but they rarely help you see pipeline volatility, new skill demands, or the downstream impact of unexpected wins and delays. This case study outlines two working prototypes that push beyond record‑keeping toward simulation and prediction: a browser‑based pipeline simulator and a curved (Bezier) hours allocator.

The problem we set out to solve
SMEs need a planning approach that's fast to set up, cheap to run, and honest about uncertainty. They want to know whether today's people will cover tomorrow's work; how to cope with stressors like client slippage, internal hiring delays, or surprise sales; and where shortfalls or surpluses will emerge as projects enter, mature, or fall out of the pipeline. Existing tools don't model those dynamics—so we built ones that do.

Simulation framework v1.0 — modeling the pipeline
The simulation is a stand‑alone JavaScript app that runs entirely in the browser. It starts with a project template: up to five colored assignment blocks, each representing a role, arranged within a 26‑week window. Planners drag to reposition or resize blocks, capturing not just how much effort a role needs, but when it's needed. Every new deal that enters the pipeline clones this template, so patterns repeat consistently across many concurrent "project instances."

Capacity is explicit. For each active role, planners set full‑time equivalents (FTEs). The system converts FTEs to hours per week (1 FTE = 40 hours) and draws per‑role and total capacity lines. As FTE counts grow, the vertical scale expands automatically. A feed‑rate control governs how frequently new project instances appear from the right, so you can simulate slow trickles or rapid booking streaks.

Uncertainty is built in. Each project lives in one of four confidence zones—25%, 50%, 75%, 100%—based on where it sits along the sales‑to‑contract timeline. As time advances, projects cross boundaries; some progress, a proportion "dies off," and only the strongest reach 100%. Visual cues reinforce this: opacity tracks confidence (a 25% prospect renders at 25% opacity), and an optional ghost view compresses curves according to cumulative confidence, yielding a more realistic picture of probable workload rather than a best‑case pile‑up.

Results are live. The simulator continuously reports elapsed time, counts of past projects, totals in each confidence band, and role‑by‑role surplus/deficit against capacity. Because it's browser‑based, teams can explore scenarios quickly without standing up a backend.

Bezier allocation — shaping hours within a project
Capacity planning also hinges on how effort unfolds. Many tools assume flat distributions; real projects rarely behave that way. Our Bezier mini‑project lets planners shape a fixed budget of hours across a timeline using a quadratic Bezier curve driven by a single control point.

Drag the point to front‑load ramp‑up, peak midstream, or taper toward delivery—the system preserves total hours, pins start and end dates, and enforces sensible slopes (positive at the start, negative at the end) so curves remain realistic. A lightweight JSON model reads/writes the project's total budget, start/end week numbers, control‑point coordinates, and computed hours per week. Axes adjust on the fly: the horizontal scale labels "Week N" across year‑end rollovers; the vertical scale adapts to whatever weekly maximum the curve produces.

How it comes together
In practice, planners define a role pattern once, feed deals into the pipeline at a chosen rate, and watch as confidence‑weighted workloads rise and fall against declared capacity. When a particular project needs a non‑flat profile, they shape its curve with the Bezier editor—no spreadsheets, no manual re‑tabulation. The combination surfaces where and when pressure accumulates, which roles will be underwater, and what happens if sales velocity or kill‑rates change.

Why this is different

  • A systems‑theory lens. Instead of static calendars, Carv models flow—entry, attrition, maturation—and makes uncertainty visible.
  • Low‑resolution, high‑yield inputs. You can start with coarse budgets, durations, and FTE counts and only add detail when it materially improves decisions.
  • A foundation for recommendations. The simulator plus Bezier shaping provide scaffolding for a future engine that forecasts surpluses/shortfalls across multiple horizons.
  • Process‑agnostic by design. Whether your delivery resembles steps, waves, or something ad hoc, the framework can mirror it—and later ingest actuals from external time logs.
  • SME‑friendly. Running in the browser keeps cost and complexity low while still enabling meaningful scenario planning.

What's next
To move from prototype to product, we'll port the simulator into the Carv React app and back it with a Django/REST API for persistence and collaboration. Confidence modeling will get tunable kill‑rates, custom boundaries, and smarter arrival distributions. The Bezier editor will support multiple control points, editable start/end dates, and reusable curve templates (e.g., discovery‑heavy vs. implementation‑heavy). On top, we'll build a recommendation layer—statistical methods and ML informed by real time‑log data—to forecast staffing risk from one week out to six months. Finally, we'll invest in UX polish: richer visuals (heat maps, subtle animations), clearer ghost views, and mobile‑friendly interactions.

Outcome
These prototypes validate that a lightweight, simulation‑first approach can answer the staffing questions SMEs actually ask. By modeling the pipeline with confidence zones and letting planners sculpt per‑project effort realistically, Carv moves past retrospective tracking toward forward‑looking capacity management—the groundwork for a scalable, affordable portfolio planning system.
